rv.q: You go in anticipating gimmicks. You leave chastened, having witnessed a searing masterpiece.
What a show – and Ryder is a star.
This is a feverish, thrilling night out - and a welcome return of the Bible belter to the West End after a long absence.
All together this is an OTT, aorta-pumping rollick through one of Lloyd Webber and Rice’s strongest musical collaborations, by a team who know that the score and the feel of it are all that matter.
Just follow Mary Magdalene’s advice – “Close your eyes, and relax” – and you’ll sink into the glorious sounds of a voice that’s achieved divine status.
It's an exciting evening but it's best not to pretend that London's latest Jesus Christ Superstar is great drama as such.
This West End revival of Tim Sheader's hit 2016 production, which reimagined Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's rock opera as an arena gig, is simultaneously amped up and hemmed in.
I’m not sure it’ll convert the unimpressed or uninitiated; but believers will love it.
This West End revival of Tim Sheader’s hit 2016 production, which reimagined Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice’s rock opera as an arena gig, is simultaneously amped up and hemmed in.
All in all it’s a good production that slots into the Jamie Lloyd era of Sexy Lloyd Webber very nicely indeed.
But dramatically it fares less well.
It’s a shame it stays at a single, fever-pitched high, flattening the emotional drama.
Tim Sheader’s rock-tastic production was first seen at Regent’s Park Open Air in 2016, and it makes a pulse-racing, soul-stirring, triumphant return.

In Timothy Sheader’s immaculate production – first seen to Olivier-winning effect at Regent’s Park 10 years ago, and harnessing Drew McOnie’s pin-sharp choreography – this is a religious leader ensnared by his own cult; there’s something frightening, if hypnotic, about his volatile, restless followers.

At the age of 56, the musical isn’t showing its age remotely, with its vigorous, unashamedly complex rhythms and persuasive interrogation of the Bible marking it as a resounding classic even for Lloyd Webber agnostics like this critic.

It takes a talented director to create a show from a soundtrack that retains huge appeal, but sometimes lacks personal story arcs. Sheader’s engaging staging and a hugely talented cast bring the album powerfully to life. … Ryder’s West End debut brings raw vulnerability and real passion to the role.
In all, a terrific effort, albeit once again over amplified.

Between Ryder’s stamina, Huntley’s silvered hands and Drew McOnie’s choreography – contemporary folded into something liturgical – this Superstar preaches convincingly to the converted and wins a few souls besides.
Sound issues aside on the night, it’s a decent and dynamic production.
This production easily becomes the frontrunner for show of the year.
This production is easily five-star.

Sheader’s production has earned its confidence the hard way, across a decade and several postcodes, and this latest stop is worth catching on the strength of everything around its reluctant, golden-voiced centre.
Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber's rock opera still possesses extraordinary theatrical energy, and in Sam Ryder, it has found a leading man capable of carrying that legacy forward.
This is an impressively staged and directed production of a musical that is sometimes brilliant and often baffling.
I left disappointed and felt that the show did not explore the music or characters in as much depth as they could have feasibly done.
The result is a show that looks consistently impressive, yet only intermittently involving.
Though it isn’t anywhere near so bad that you could say the show has been crucified, it’s fair to say this version of Jesus Christ Superstar doesn’t quite manage to exceed expectations.
This production will have a rotating cast of King Herod, and I’m delighted that this night it’s Jesse Tyler Ferguson bringing a lightly camp Short King energy.
Add in a charismatic leading performance from Sam Ryder, and this is a production well worth seeing.
It is an evening that feels more like an uneven, slightly muted concert than a fully realised, transcendent piece of musical theatre.

cn.t: Sheader's thrilling production of Lloyd Webber and Rice's rock opera earns praise for its high-octane energy, spectacular staging, and Sam Ryder's charismatic star turn as Jesus, proving the 1970s musical remains a powerful, pulse-racing classic.

lo.inst: Enter via show website. Draws Thursdays at 12 PM.
